newsitem.title: FRANCE: French pilots strike, farmers protest.
newsitem.headline: French pilots strike, farmers protest.

text.p: Pilots at national airline Air France and its short-haul division Air France Europe went on a four-day strike on Tuesday, but the airlines said they hoped disruption would be limited.
Air France was maintaining its flight schedule, but some disruption as possible on European and domestic flights.

The strike is to protest against planned wage cuts for new pilots and changes in working conditions under a merger between the two airlines in order to make them more competitive as European airlines are opened up to cross-border competition.
Air France Chairman Christian Blanc has urged pilots to ignore the strike, saying it would wipe out the airline's entire year profit and endanger the future of the state-owned airline.

Air France accuses the unions of stoking the conflict by calling a strike while negotiations are under way on the points of disagreement. It believes many of the pilots and flight engineers oppose the strike and will not participate.

Air France wants to hire 450 pilots in the next year and a half and would pay them gross starting salaries of 220,000 francs ($38,260) a year, a third less than what was paid to the pilots now on staff.
The SNPL pilots union said an independent study shows the wages proposed for new pilots at the state-owned group are lower than those paid by Lufthansa , British Airways and KLM.
The SNCF state railway company said train traffic was near normal after a six-day strike by train conductors. Disruption was limited to some inter-regional lines.
About one in three trains had been cancelled on most main lines between Wednesday and Sunday in the dispute over staffing levels and bonuses.
The stoppage had spared high-speed Eurostar trains to London through the Channel Tunnel.
In another protest, dairy farmers blocked deliveries to hypermarkets in various parts of France, accusing big distribution firms of gradually bringing down milk prices.
They set up roadblocks before dawn and turned back delivery trucks.

"We cannot accept a downwards price spiral until 2000, because we would never regain what we would have lost," a union spokesman said. He called for the government to set up a crisis unit to discuss farmers' grievances.
Asked about the protest, Prime Minister Alain Juppe told RTL radio it could be settled by talks. "Conflicts are solved through talks...We have solved many of them," he said.
